A task-irrelevant but highly salient visual onset presented before search will reactivate the previous target location with comparable neural selectivity to a valid goal-directed cue, demonstrating that stimulus-driven engagement of the priority map is sufficient to release activity-silent selection-history traces.

Engaging the stimulus-driven layer of the priority map will reactivate latent history-driven priority, such that a salient but task-irrelevant distractor presented at the previous target location will produce stronger attentional capture and a larger reactivated neural representation of that previous target than a distractor at a neutral location, even when current goal-directed attention is directed elsewhere.
